Open HTTP response begins → Frames metadata + content deltas → Finish reason: stop or limit → [DONE] terminal SSE marker Strict completion rule for this course's raw-SSE probe. A socket close after content but before the expected terminal marker is a partial stream, not an ordinary complete answer. Verify the exact protocol for the installed server version. A proxy can buffer or coalesce frames, changing the client's first-content time without changing engine computation. It can also time out or close a stream after several deltas. The application should distinguish an intentionally complete answer from a partial one and avoid saving partial text as if it passed the same quality check. A retry after partial delivery needs its own idempotency and user-interface policy; repeating generation may produce different text. Chapter 01's observer-clock lesson applies again: capture server emission and client receipt separately before blaming decode. One complete CPU example: bytes become text, lines and events Server-sent events, abbreviated SSE, define a text framing format. The format does not imply that each network read contains one event, that each event contains one token, or that each token corresponds to one Unicode character. Separate all four units before writing a parser. A socket supplies bytes. UTF-8 maps bytes into Unicode text. Line endings divide that text into fields. A blank line dispatches an SSE event. Only then can an application interpret the event’s data as a JSON object or the API-specific terminal string [DONE] . The WHATWG event-stream specification defines framing; the pinned vLLM chat implementation defines its chat payloads. The following request and stream are synthetic CPU fixtures . No model produced their content, timings or usage counters. Their purpose is to make every parser state inspectable without downloads, CUDA or a running service. The notebook embeds the same fixture JSON and standard-library parser. The question is deliberately different from the historical server smoke, so a reader cannot accidentally attach old GPU timings to it. {JSON.stringify(fixture.request,null,2)} The text deltas concatenate in arrival order to Café ☕. . The role event has empty content. The finish event ends generation, the usage event reports accounting, and the final data event contains [DONE] . A leading heartbeat comment is a framed record but produces no application data event. Consequently this fixture has seven records including the comment, six data events, five JSON objects, two content events and sixteen supplied byte chunks. The invented usage counter says four completion tokens. Those are five different counts with different meanings, not alternative spellings of “tokens.” Inspect the entire fixture wire text Visible \r\n below denotes the two line-ending characters. A second line ending closes each event. The actual fixture uses those bytes, not four printable backslash letters. {fixture.frames.map((frame,index)=>`Record ${index+1}\n${frame.replaceAll('\r','\\r').replaceAll('\n','\\n\n')}`).join('\n')} A chunk can end halfway through é In UTF-8, é occupies the two bytes C3 A9 , and ☕ occupies E2 98 95 . One network read can end after C3 ; the next can begin with A9 . Decoding the first read independently with strict UTF-8 fails because the sequence is incomplete. Decoding it with replacement mode may insert a replacement character and irreversibly damage the JSON string. An incremental decoder retains the unfinished byte prefix and combines it with the next read. The same reasoning applies to the three-byte coffee character, which the fixture deliberately splits after E2 . Chunk boundaries are accidental transport observations. A proxy, TLS record, OS buffer or HTTP client implementation can change them without changing the logical event stream. The classroom fixture supplies sixteen chunks to stress this fact. Joining every chunk first and parsing at EOF would recover the same final text, but would defeat streaming and make first-content measurements meaningless. A correct streaming client processes complete events as soon as enough bytes arrive while preserving every incomplete suffix for the next read. Line buffering and event dispatch SSE accepts LF, CRLF or CR line endings. CRLF may itself split between reads, so the parser needs to remember a trailing CR and avoid interpreting the following LF as an extra blank line. A line beginning with a colon is a comment. A field such as data: hello contributes hello to the event’s data buffer; the parser removes at most one optional space after the colon. Two data lines become one data value separated by newline. The next blank line dispatches the assembled event. Unknown fields do not become JSON content merely because they arrived on the same connection. For example, data: &#123;"choices":[], followed by data: "usage":&#123;"prompt_tokens":13,"completion_tokens":4,"total_tokens":17&#125;&#125; and a blank line forms one JSON document with a newline after its comma. Calling json.loads on either data line independently fails. Conversely, a single network read may contain two whole events, and a parser that stops after the first loses data. The notebook tests both split and coalesced input. At EOF, the parser must not dispatch an event that never reached its blank-line terminator. A minimal processing sketch is below. It names state rather than hiding it inside a library. The actual notebook implementation additionally validates JSON shape, choice index, byte limits, trailing input, usage fields and invalid UTF-8. Its scope is a single text choice. It does not implement browser reconnection, arbitrary event handlers, tools, audio, multimodal output or every provider’s stream dialect. {`for byte_chunk in incoming_reads: decoded_text = utf8_decoder.feed(byte_chunk) for complete_line in line_buffer.feed(decoded_text): if complete_line is a comment: continue if complete_line is a data field: event_data.append(field_value) if complete_line is blank: payload = join_data_lines_with_newline(event_data) event_data.clear() if payload == "[DONE]": mark_terminal() elif payload: update_client_state(parse_json(payload)) on_eof: reject_invalid_utf8_or_unterminated_data() classify_using_finish_done_and_error_state()`} Protocol completion, output quality and cancellation Keep at least the accumulated content, finish reason, usage object, terminal-marker flag and error state. A role event can initialize metadata without appending text. A nonempty content delta appends exactly its string; trimming every delta would turn Café plus ☕. into Café☕. . An empty choices list can carry usage and must not trigger choices[0] . A finish reason can arrive before the final accounting event, so stopping immediately at finish discards legitimate trailing metadata. Under the course’s strict one-choice text contract, normal completion requires a recognized finish reason, terminal [DONE] , valid stream shape and no recorded error. finish_reason="stop" usually indicates the generation reached its stopping condition. finish_reason="length" indicates a cap stopped it. Either can terminate a syntactically complete stream, but a length-limited answer may be unacceptable for the task. A parser should retain the reason, while the application decides whether the answer satisfies its requirements. A calculator demanding one integer can reject fluent prose after a normal stop. A summarizer can reject a sentence cut in half after a length stop. A tool-calling application requires a different success predicate from this chapter’s text-only client. The API may send an error object after HTTP headers already declared success. At that point, the server cannot revise the already transmitted status code. The pinned vLLM implementation can emit an error event and then [DONE] . Therefore the terminal marker alone cannot mean successful generation. Preserve the error even when DONE arrives afterward. A stream with plausible partial text and no DONE is likewise incomplete under this course contract. Saving that text as a fully accepted result corrupts both the user experience and the success denominator. Fixture variant Client observation Classification What it does not establish All events Content, stop, usage, DONE Complete protocol response Model quality or real server health Drop terminal event Same text, no DONE Partial That generation finished successfully Cancel after first content Café , local cancel Cancelled Engine KV state has been released Invalid JSON or error object Malformed or failed response Failed A useful complete answer The correct timestamp depends on the question For the synthetic fixture, the first data event arrives at 0.03 seconds but contains only the assistant role. First content arrives at 0.10 seconds, another content event arrives at 0.14, finish at 0.15, usage at 0.16 and DONE at 0.17. If send time is zero, first-content delay equals 0.10 − 0 = 0.10 s , or 100 ms. Terminal wall time equals 170 ms. An empty heartbeat at 10 ms does not become a first-token measurement merely because it is the first transport activity. These are illustrative client arrivals supplied by the fixture, not measurements of vLLM. The 40 ms difference between the two text events is an inter-event interval. It cannot establish token latency because the two strings may each encode multiple model tokens. Even when the server exposes token IDs, buffering may group their client arrivals. To compute a mean of known token-arrival gaps, state that there are N observed token timestamps, use (where and are the first and last token-arrival times), and retain the complete arrival sequence if studying jitter. With 40 tokens, first arrival at 0.40 s and last at 1.18 s, the illustrative mean is 0.78/39 = 0.020 s/gap . A DONE event at 1.20 s adds 20 ms of terminal processing; substituting it for the last-token timestamp mixes two quantities. Neither calculation isolates GPU decode. A client timeout does not prove engine cancellation A connection deadline limits establishing the route. A first-content deadline limits waiting for useful text. A read-inactivity timeout limits the interval without incoming transport progress. A total deadline limits the entire attempt. These clocks answer different questions and may expire at different times. An SDK timeout parameter is not automatically a whole-request wall budget; inspect its HTTP client semantics. Record the expired clock, preserve partial content with its incomplete status, and close the response in a cleanup path. Never substitute zero for an unavailable first-content time. Closing the client stream is the first step in cancellation. The frontend and any proxy must observe the disconnect, propagate an abort for the relevant request, and release live engine state. A client-only fixture can prove that the application labels an attempt cancelled, but cannot prove that a real GPU worker stopped generating or released KV blocks. That needs engine-side active-request evidence, resource recovery and, ideally, a follow-up bounded smoke. The historical course run did not contain a cancellation experiment, so cancellation cleanup remains a proposed test rather than a measured success. Browser EventSource adds automatic reconnect behavior around a GET request. This chapter uses an HTTP POST carrying a JSON generation request and reads its response as SSE. Copying EventSource’s reconnect policy blindly into this client can start another generation, duplicate text or replay tool side effects. A retry is a new attempt unless an explicitly supported application protocol proves otherwise. Keep its attempt ID and metrics separate. After partial display, decide whether to replace the old answer, offer a user-controlled retry, or visibly preserve the partial answer. Appending a regenerated answer to the first one is usually a bug. Worked incident: healthy generation, delayed delivery Consider an illustrative observation: direct loopback receives its first content at 100 ms and successive events afterward, while an external client receives all events near 900 ms. This pattern suggests buffering somewhere on the external path, but does not prove which component caused it. Compare the same prompt, model, sampling settings and request correlation fields. Inspect server emission spans and proxy configuration without subtracting unsynchronized wall clocks from different machines. Test the direct and proxied paths separately, with one bounded request each. If the proxy buffers by block, changing that policy and rerunning the paired test should change client arrival shape while leaving engine work comparable. A successful local probe does not certify remote timeouts, authentication, TLS or cancellation propagation. Equally, a slow remote first-content time does not justify increasing GPU memory utilization before inspecting the route. Write the diagnosis as a falsifiable hypothesis: “The proxy holds events until its buffer flushes.” Evidence against it could be late engine emission even on the direct route. The purpose of the service map is to find this next discriminating measurement, not to assign every delay to the nearest unfamiliar component. A useful negative test is an expected failure The wrong-model and over-context probes deliberately produce non-2xx responses. They are not “failed lab runs”; they test that invalid input is rejected at a predictable boundary. For the wrong-model request, 404 points first to the served-name contract. For the 2,329-token rendered prompt against a 2,048-token cap, 400 points to validation of a declared size limit. The latter is better than allowing impossible work to consume GPU memory until an obscure worker error occurs. A 500-class error or transport disconnect on a valid request would be a different incident and should not be merged with these expected negatives in a “failure rate” denominator. When writing automated checks, assert the status, the relevant response shape, and the reason the input should fail. Do not merely assert “not 200.” Otherwise a broken server that returns 500 for every request would pass the negative suite. Positive and negative probes belong together: model list, ordinary chat, stream completion, wrong identity and over-context jointly test a small observable contract. Their combined success is a strong smoke result and a weak capacity result—exactly the distinction the chapter intends to teach. Context is a memory policy, not merely a string length Count rendered tokens after applying the exact chat template, then add the requested output cap before judging a model-length limit. Long prompts also create KV state; a request-count cap alone cannot guarantee fit. The KV budget explorer shows the logical payload arithmetic, but it omits vLLM’s allocator and runtime reserves. The engine arguments document context and memory controls; the run record states which values this course actually used. Worked context calculation: reject before expensive work The server launch set --max-model-len 2048 . The negative probe's chat template produced 2,329 prompt tokens. The prompt alone exceeded the configured limit by 2329 − 2048 = 281 tokens, so rejecting it with HTTP 400 was a valid, inexpensive outcome; no amount of queue patience could make that request fit the declared context. A different illustrative request with 1,800 rendered prompt tokens and a 512-token output cap asks for up to 2,312 total positions, also beyond 2,048, though its input alone fits. An application should make this distinction visible instead of telling every 400 caller only “bad request.” The first pair is measured; the second is a worked example. The limit applies after rendering roles and template markers Scenario Rendered prompt Requested output cap Against 2,048 Pinned negative probe 2,329 Not needed to exceed 281 over; observed HTTP 400 Illustrative chat 1,800 512 2,312 potential; 264 over Illustrative smaller chat 1,800 128 1,928 potential; 120 spare Only the first row is a measured API response. Actual admitted-generation accounting follows the installed runtime's rules; the worked rows teach why output budget belongs in the context decision. A request-count cap is not a memory proof The launch also set --max-num-seqs 4 and --gpu-memory-utilization 0.45 . Four is an upper bound on simultaneously active sequences in that configuration, not an achieved client throughput or evidence that four maximum-length sequences were ever present. From the pinned 0.5B model config , 24 layers, two KV heads and a 64-dimensional head at two bytes per value give 2 × 24 × 2 × 64 × 2 = 12,288 bytes = 12 KiB of logical FP16 KV payload per retained token. Four hypothetical full 2,048-token sequences would hold 4 × 2048 × 12 KiB = 96 MiB of logical KV payload. This is not the service's allocated VRAM: model weights, runtime reservation, block accounting, graph buffers and other tensors remain. The arithmetic also does not imply that a 45% memory-utilization target is “mostly unused GPU.” Engine flags control an allocator budget and runtime behavior; memory visible in a device monitor may include reserved pools. A cap of four sequences can prevent the instructor smoke from overcommitting a host but tells us little about a different model or a 64-client workload. To design a real admission envelope, measure peak live and reserved memory across the intended context distribution and check failures as clients increase. Chapter 02's KV calculation is a component ledger, not a license to set request count by division alone. Diagnose the boundary before touching flags A small decision tree for common client symptoms Symptom First discriminating check Likely boundary if confirmed Do not assume 404 with valid route Compare client model string with /v1/models . Served model identity GPU failure. 400 on chat Inspect rendered prompt count, output cap and template error. Validation / template Every 400 means context overflow. Content deltas then disconnect Was finish reason and [DONE] observed? Stream completion / transport Partial text is complete. Valid request times out Locate queue, engine and client spans; inspect resource limits. Admission, worker or transport The last visible component caused the delay. Diagnostic starting points, not exhaustive HTTP semantics. Preserve the full response and server trace ID before restarting or changing the model. Run it weekly without starting from zero Keep pinned model snapshots and package environments in the project-local cache. Start only one bounded GPU process at a time on the instructor host, preflight available RAM and GPU headroom, and stop the service cleanly after tests. A clean process restart does not require deleting immutable model weights and downloading them again. Keep secrets, private prompts, and unsanitized logs out of public evidence. The course’s public submission example carries only student-facing artifacts. Weekly repetition should reuse assets, not stale processes A repeatable lab has two different kinds of state. Immutable model snapshots, pinned packages and declared benchmark inputs can be prefetched once into a durable project-local cache. Running servers, sockets, GPU allocations and temporary output files are disposable and should be recreated or cleaned between attempts. Deleting the whole cache to get a “clean run” forces a network download, adds nondeterminism and wastes the course window; retaining a dead worker to save startup time risks stale ports and memory. The instructor procedure verifies cached revisions in offline mode before launching one bounded GPU process at a time. The Topic 04 smoke used loopback-only host 127.0.0.1 , port 8000 , FP16, a 2,048-token model length, at most four active sequences, a 0.45 GPU-memory-utilization target and eager execution. These settings protected and stabilized this one WSL2 teaching run; they are not production defaults to copy without measuring. The run completed in a bounded process, and the GPU and port were released afterward. If a later session finds the port still occupied or GPU memory above baseline, that is a preflight failure to investigate before starting another server, not a reason to stack a second process on the same device. The launch command as a reproducibility record {launch} &lt;PINNED_LOCAL_SNAPSHOT&gt; is an explanatory placeholder, not a literal shell path. The notebook resolves the verified local snapshot and passes arguments as a list, avoiding shell interpretation of a path. --served-model-name fixes the API identity. --host 127.0.0.1 binds to the loopback interface. --dtype float16 declares the model compute/storage choice supported by this run. --max-model-len 2048 establishes the context cap. --max-num-seqs 4 limits sequences processed in one iteration according to the vLLM 0.29.0 CLI reference ; it is not four requests per second or a cap on every connected client. --gpu-memory-utilization 0.45 controls an executor memory budget. --enforce-eager chooses the eager execution path for this bounded teaching run. These flags interact with model configuration, runtime defaults and hardware. A reported memory percentage is not the logical KV size, and a successful startup is not proof that every admitted workload fits. Save the installed runtime version and effective configuration beside the command. The historical WSL2 host used a V1-runner/native-sampler fallback. Keep that workaround scoped to the recorded environment instead of publishing it as a universal performance recommendation. Reusing an already matching package environment is appropriate; blindly reinstalling on every notebook restart wastes time and introduces a second failure source. Health, readiness and the first successful request Readiness is a decision for a particular consumer. A process existence check finds an early crash but does not demonstrate a listener. A TCP connection demonstrates reachability but may terminate at a proxy. A health endpoint in the pinned implementation checks engine health, while /v1/models exposes configured identities. Neither exercises the exact chat template and output contract. The notebook therefore follows a bounded readiness wait with identity verification and a small complete chat request. A health check is useful evidence without being a substitute for this sequence. Bound the wait with a monotonic deadline. If the process exits, report the exit and local log path immediately rather than sleeping until the deadline. If readiness never arrives, terminate only the server process tree owned by this run and verify cleanup before another attempt. Preserve the first failure and its context. Repeatedly restarting a worker while discarding logs creates a loop that can consume RAM, leave stale ports and conceal the original error. A missing model snapshot should fail before server startup when the session is meant to run offline. What a useful service artifact must let another reader check The lab artifact is more than a screenshot of text. It identifies the model repository, immutable revision, tokenizer, served name, runtime versions and launch arguments. Each probe records its own request settings and observed outcome. A successful ordinary request retains content, finish reason, usage when provided and wall time. A streaming request retains first-content time, completion state and enough sanitized events to distinguish a full response from a partial one. Expected-negative probes retain the exact status and reason. Startup and cleanup evidence describe process and resource state separately from request latency. For the new CPU path, retain the fixture version, reconstructed output and classifications of complete, partial, malformed and cancelled variants. They prove parser behavior, not a live endpoint. For the GPU path, students independently arrange a CUDA GPU and run the bounded smoke. A CPU-only replay cannot satisfy that requirement. Questions containing logs or repository access details belong in the private student repository’s Issue with @levshaazz ; general questions without private data can use the public template’s Issues. Avoid placing API keys, local usernames, private prompts or environment dumps in the submitted public-facing excerpts. A bounded service rehearsal has a stop condition at each stage Stage Observation to record Stop rather than continue when… Preflight Snapshot revisions, offline cache verification, RAM/GPU headroom, free port A required asset is missing or resource headroom is unsafe. Startup Runtime version, flags, readiness, server PID and log location Readiness misses its bounded deadline or worker fails. Positive smoke Model list, ordinary chat, complete SDK/raw stream Identity, content or terminal marker is wrong. Expected negatives Wrong-model 404 and over-context 400 with reason Invalid requests unexpectedly reach the worker or return 500. Teardown Server stopped, port released, GPU use back to baseline Resources remain held; do not start the next GPU task. Teaching-operator sequence derived from the course's bounded rehearsal practice. It is distinct from the private grading reference run, which has its own preflight, provenance and publication contract. A compatible API is not automatically a safe public API The local smoke binds to loopback. Exposing an endpoint to students or the internet adds authentication, network policy, rate limits, tenant isolation, logging/privacy rules and abuse handling. An OpenAI-compatible request schema does not supply those protections on its own. Do not place an API key in a slide, notebook output, screenshot, URL query string or public repository. Redact private prompts and client identifiers before publishing traces. A reproducible teaching example can share model revision, workload shape, status codes and sanitized responses without revealing secrets or private grading inputs. Also distinguish API compatibility from exact behavioral identity. Two servers may accept the same chat-completions JSON yet differ in supported optional fields, chat-template defaults, tool-call behavior, error bodies or token accounting. Pin the installed release and test the fields your application actually uses. The instructor smoke exercises a small core: model list, ordinary chat, streaming completion and two negative cases. A product that depends on tools, JSON schema, parallel calls or long context needs its own contract tests; passing this chapter's probes is a foundation, not certification of every OpenAI API feature. Do not turn a five-probe smoke into a capacity claim The historical 29 September non-streamed wall time of 0.748 seconds and separate streamed 0.463 seconds are observable, but they have no latency distribution. The stream's 0.053-second first content does not establish p95 TTFT. The server's four-sequence cap does not establish four requests per second, let alone behavior at 64 clients. For a capacity claim, declare an arrival process, input/output distribution, duration, deadline and success rules; sweep bounded load while measuring all attempts, goodput, successful latency distributions, rejects, timeouts and resource headroom. Preserve raw records and check teardown at each stage. That work belongs to the benchmark/serving-performance curriculum, not to this API-contract smoke. This limitation is useful in incident triage. If a valid request intermittently times out, do not cite the 0.748-second smoke as proof that the model “should be fast.” Compare the actual workload and concurrent live-token state with the smoke. If the problem is a wrong served name, a long load test is wasted effort; if the model list is correct but p95 collapses at load, another isolated SDK hello-world is equally uninformative. Each probe should falsify a hypothesis at the appropriate layer. Exercises and answer reasoning /v1/models returns topic04 , but the client sends a different model string and receives 404. Give the different meanings of a repository ID, immutable revision, local snapshot path and served model name. Which belongs in the chat JSON? The parser receives one byte chunk ending in C3 and the next beginning in A9 . What state must survive between chunks, and what can go wrong with replacement decoding? How many records, data events, JSON objects, content events and supplied byte chunks does the synthetic fixture contain? Why does its invented completion-token counter differ? For an illustrative prompt of 1,800 rendered tokens under a 2,048 cap, compare output caps 512 and 128. What can you conclude before executing either request? The runtime sets --max-num-seqs 4 . Does that mean four users, four requests/second, four active requests at every context, or a scheduling limit? Explain the evidence still needed for capacity. In the historical 29 September record, ordinary wall time is 0.748 s and separate SDK first content is 0.053 s. Can their difference identify decode time? Could either number be called p95? This 404 is an identity-contract result and gives no evidence of GPU slowness or failure. 2329 − 2048 = 281 tokens over the declared cap before any output budget. Compare first engine-emitted content with first client-visible content under one request ID, plus the terminal event; avoid subtracting unsynchronized host wall clocks. 2 × 24 × 2 × 64 × 2 = 12,288 bytes = 12 KiB/token ; 4 × 2048 × 12 KiB = 96 MiB of idealized logical KV. This does not measure actual live sequences or total process VRAM and does not establish throughput. Verify cached pinned assets offline and resource headroom; launch one bounded loopback service; run positive and expected-negative probes; terminate and verify port/GPU baseline; keep sanitized evidence and discard disposable process state. A count alone cannot reconstruct IDs. The repository ID locates the upstream artifact, the immutable revision identifies a version of its files, the snapshot path locates the local copy, and the served name selects an API identity. This client sends the advertised name topic04 . The server, not the remote client, uses the local snapshot path. The incremental UTF-8 decoder retains pending C3 until A9 completes é . Decoding each read separately can raise an error or insert a replacement character. In either case a valid logical stream can become a corrupted client result. Line and event buffers must survive read boundaries too. Seven records including the heartbeat, six data events, five JSON objects, two content events and sixteen byte chunks. At the blank-line event boundary, join data fields with a newline and then parse the complete JSON value. EOF before that boundary leaves an incomplete event, which the client does not dispatch as a completed payload. The stream also needs its completion conditions; EOF itself supplies none. First data event: 30 ms. First content: 100 ms. Terminal wall time: 170 ms. The course first-content delay is 100 ms. A device monitor alone may include reserved pools, so use engine state as well. The historical smoke did not establish this chain. These calculations identify a planned budget mismatch and remaining logical positions. They do not prove the exact installed server response, quality, memory fit or latency of either request. The pinned flag limits sequences processed in one iteration. It does not promise any request rate, every-context fit or a fixed number of HTTP connections. A capacity claim needs a declared workload distribution, arrival process, success/timeout policy, repeated outcomes and resource observations. No on both counts. They come from separate requests and observer intervals. Their subtraction does not recover one request’s decode phase. A single observation has no measured p95 distribution, and rounding does not create one. If valid stop and length terminations count as protocol success while errors do not, the share is 3/5=60% . If task policy rejects the capped answer, accepted-answer share is 2/5=40% . The partial and error attempts remain in the denominator. Declare the cap policy before measuring. The rendering/tokenizer/template boundary is implicated after frontend identity and basic engine checks. Correct the pinned template or model choice, inspect the exact rendered input, then run one small complete chat request using the intended roles. A plain completion request bypasses part of this contract and cannot replace it. Hypothesis: an intermediary buffers SSE until a size or time threshold. Compare direct/proxied arrival shapes with matched inputs and correlated server emission spans. Late engine emission on the direct route would refute buffering as the sole explanation. Avoid subtracting unsynchronized host clocks. Terms used in this chapter Served model name The API-facing identifier advertised to clients, independent of a local filesystem path. Chat template The model-specific rendering rule that places roles, message content and generation delimiters before tokenization. UTF-8 A variable-width encoding of Unicode text into bytes. One character can cross network-read boundaries. SSE event A dispatched event assembled from text fields and a blank-line boundary. Its data is not inherently a model token. Delta An incremental update, such as a fragment of content or metadata. Append content exactly, preserving spaces. Finish reason The generation-level reason an output ended, distinct from the terminal transport marker. First-content delay The client interval from sending the request to the first nonempty generated text delta. Readiness An operational decision that this deployment can serve the declared client contract, supported by appropriate probes. Cancellation A request to stop an in-flight attempt. Client classification and actual server resource release require different evidence. Smoke test A small bounded test of a declared path. It can reveal broken integration without estimating capacity or quality over a population. The next topic opens the engine boundary: how live sequences share KV blocks and how the scheduler admits work at iteration boundaries. Here the deliverable is the observable client and lifecycle contract that makes those later measurements interpretable.

Glossary

Quantization scale

Reconstruction step or scale factor. In an affine integer toy it has weight-value units per code; q = clip(round(w/s) + z), reconstructed w = s(q − z).

Glossary

Zero point

Integer code that represents zero in an affine quantizer. It is a representation parameter, not the floating-point scale or a model bias.

Glossary

Nibble

Four bits. Two INT4 codes can share one byte, but nibble order, signed encoding, padding and logical tensor shape must be specified.

Glossary

NF4

NormalFloat4: sixteen nonuniform reconstruction levels, used with block scales in the lab. Four bits do not imply the same codebook, packing or kernel as signed INT4.

Glossary

Paired discordance

Prompt-level outcomes on which two candidates disagree. Equal aggregate success rates can hide different regressions and gains.

Glossary

SSE data event

Data dispatched after a blank line. One network read can contain many events or part of one; an event can contain several tokens or no text.

Glossary

Finish reason

Application field explaining why generation ended. It is distinct from the terminal DONE marker, connection EOF and validation of the answer's usefulness.

Glossary

Incremental UTF-8 decoding

Decoding that retains incomplete multibyte characters across byte reads, so splitting a character at a transport boundary does not corrupt its text.

Glossary

Residual stream

The hidden vector carried at each position. Attention and MLP branches add updates to it; the retained KV cache is separate state.

Glossary

RMSNorm

Per-position normalization using the root mean square over hidden features, epsilon and a learned feature scale. It does not mix sequence positions or subtract their mean.

Glossary

RoPE

Rotary positional embedding: position-dependent rotations of paired query/key coordinates. In this Qwen implementation values are not rotated.

Glossary

SwiGLU

A gated feed-forward branch: apply SiLU to the gate projection, multiply elementwise by a separate up projection, then project down to the residual width.

Glossary

Logits

Unnormalized vocabulary scores. Greedy decoding selects their largest entry; softmax probabilities are not a measure of factual confidence.

Glossary

Admission control

Decision to accept, queue, shed, or defer a request before it consumes scarce serving capacity.

Glossary

Arithmetic intensity

Operations performed per byte moved at the memory level being modeled.

Glossary

Continuous batching

Scheduler that can change the active request batch between decode iterations.

Glossary

Decode

Autoregressive phase that produces new tokens one iteration at a time using cached keys and values.

Glossary

Failure rate

Failed requests divided by all attempted requests under the declared workload and timeout.

Glossary

GQA

Grouped-query attention: multiple query heads share fewer key/value heads.

Glossary

ITL

Inter-token latency: time between two consecutive streamed output tokens for one request.

Glossary

KV cache

Per-request key/value state retained from earlier tokens to avoid recomputing attention history.

Glossary

Little’s Law

For a stable system, average concurrency equals arrival rate times average time in system: L=λW.

Glossary

Operational intensity

Measured operations per byte at a chosen boundary; used to place work on a roofline chart.

Glossary

Quantization

Mapping high-precision values into a lower-bit representation with a reconstruction rule, metadata and error.

Glossary

AWQ

Activation-aware weight quantization: uses activation statistics to protect salient channels through scaling.

Glossary

GPTQ

Post-training weight quantization that uses approximate second-order information to compensate quantization error.

Glossary

Served model name

The API-facing model identifier advertised by /v1/models and sent in the client's model field.

Glossary

SSE

Server-sent events: UTF-8 event framing over HTTP. The vLLM chat application adds JSON deltas and a DONE marker; these are not universal SSE protocol fields.

Glossary

Prefill

Parallel processing of prompt tokens that builds initial KV state and produces the first-token logits.

Glossary

Roofline

Upper-bound performance model combining compute and bandwidth ceilings; not a full latency predictor.

Glossary

SLO

Service-level objective: a measurable reliability or performance target over a defined population and window.

Glossary

Tail latency

A high percentile such as p95 or p99, always meaningful only with its population and failure semantics.

Glossary

TPOT

Time per output token after the first, usually decode duration divided by post-first-token gaps; not one individual ITL.

Glossary

TTFT

Time from the declared request start boundary until the first output token becomes observable.

Glossary

CUDA event interval

Elapsed time between device events on a stream; may include launch gaps and is not a sum of kernel durations.

Glossary

Allocated vs reserved memory

Allocated memory holds live tensors; reserved memory also includes blocks retained by the caching allocator. Neither is total device usage.

Glossary

Kernel interval union

Total time covered by at least one recorded physical kernel interval, counting overlaps once. It excludes other unrecorded activity.

Glossary

Warmup

Unreported execution of the actual shape/path before timed trials; not permission to discard slow measured repeats.

Glossary

Clipping

Mapping a value outside the representable range to an endpoint; distinguish it from rounding within the range.

Slide L00

Premise

" Training cooks the dish once. Serving cooks it for everyone, every night — and the guests all arrive at seven. the premise of this course A model that answers one prompt in two seconds on your laptop is a demo. A service that answers two hundred people at once, with a predictable first-token delay, without running out of memory, at a known cost per million tokens — that is what this course builds. The trail is the course in four stones: one stove, a better cooking system (vLLM), more stoves (multi-GPU), more kitchens (Kubernetes).

Slide L00

The naive kitchen

The naive kitchen transformers.pipeline behind a web server is this kitchen: every order is cooked perfectly — one at a time . This is how most first deployments look: wrap pipeline() in FastAPI, put a lock around generate(), ship. It works beautifully for one user. Next slide: what the 64th guest experiences.

Slide L00

When the k-th guest gets the answer

When the k-th guest gets the answer Back-of-the-envelope · step with → Assume one answer = 256 output tokens, and the naive server generates 40 tokens/s for a single request → 6.4 s per order. Orders are served strictly one after another. 01 1 client Nobody waits. Looks production-ready. 6.4 s 02 8 clients Seven orders are cooked before it, then its own: \(8 \times 6.4\) s. 51 s 03 32 clients \(32 \times 6.4\) s. Most HTTP clients and load balancers time out around here. 3.4 min 04 64 clients \(64 \times 6.4\) s. The compute units were under-utilized while each decode step repeatedly streamed model weights from memory — the next two slides show why. 6.8 min Illustrative numbers, not measurements — the live demo measures the real ones on a Colab T4. The point is the shape: with a serial server, the wait of the k-th client grows linearly in k, while the throughput stays flat. Adding clients adds only waiting, not work done. Ask: is the GPU busy during these 6.8 minutes? Hold the answer for two slides.

Slide L00

Why one order at a time wastes the stove

Why one order at a time wastes the stove Every decode step reads all the weights $$ t_{\text{step}} \;\gtrsim\; \frac{\text{bytes of weights}}{\text{memory bandwidth}} \;=\; \frac{8\ \text{GB}}{896\ \text{GB/s}} \;\approx\; 9\ \text{ms} $$ B = 1 One token per step for one request → ≤ ~110 tokens/s , no matter how fast the math units are. B = 64 The same weight read serves 64 requests → ceiling ~64× higher , until compute or memory runs out. ⇒ Batching is cheap in weight traffic during decode. Compute, KV traffic and scheduling still grow. Example: a 4B-parameter model in BF16 = 8 GB of weights; the judge GPU (RTX 5070 Ti) has about 896 GB/s of memory bandwidth. To produce one token, the GPU has to stream every weight from memory once: ≈ 9 ms. So a single request is capped near 110 tokens/s — the arithmetic units sit mostly idle, waiting for memory. If 64 requests decode in the same step, the weight traffic can be amortized across the batch. That does not make batching free: matrix compute, KV-cache reads and writes, scheduling work and memory capacity all grow, and the workload eventually becomes compute-bound or runs out of KV cache. This is a lower bound on step time and an upper bound on speed — real numbers are lower. Topic 2 does this properly (roofline, arithmetic intensity).

Slide L00

Common misconception

Common misconception Bust the myth What people think &ldquo;Our LLM is slow under load. We need a faster GPU.&rdquo; Reveal truth Under load, a serial server is limited by scheduling and memory , not by FLOPs. A GPU with twice the memory bandwidth halves the 6.8-minute wait to 3.4 minutes. Serving all 64 orders together — continuous batching, a well-managed KV cache — turns minutes into seconds on the same GPU . That is the whole course in one sentence. Get the misconception out loud first — ask who would buy the bigger GPU. Then reveal. The rest of the course is the set of software moves that make the same hardware serve an order of magnitude more people.

Slide L00

The catch: counter space

The catch: counter space Every live order keeps its KV cache in VRAM $$ \text{KV per token} \;=\; 2 \times L \times H_{kv} \times d_h \times \text{bytes} $$ 2 a key and a value vector per head \(L \cdot H_{kv} \cdot d_h\) layers × KV heads × head size: \(36 \times 8 \times 128\) for a 4B-class model = 144 KiB per token in FP16 (2 bytes) — kept for every token of every live request The arithmetic: 2 (K and V) × 36 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 head dimension × 2 bytes = 147 456 bytes ≈ 144 KiB per token. A representative 4B-class configuration; your model's config.json gives its own L, H_kv and d_h. The KV cache grows with every prompt token and every generated token, for every request that is in flight. Next slide: what that means inside 16 GB.

Slide L00

16 GB of VRAM, budgeted

16 GB of VRAM, budgeted Batching amortizes weight traffic — but consumes compute and memory Weights, 4B in BF16 8 GB Runtime, activations ~2 GB Left for the KV cache ~6 GB ÷ 144 KiB per token ≈ 40 000 tokens ÷ 64 guests ≈ 630 tokens each ! 630 tokens is prompt + answer The leaderboard load is 64 × (512 + 256) ≈ 49 000 tokens. This setup does not fit it — the scheduler makes guests wait or evicts someone. i Every lever buys counter space Quantized weights and KV cache, PagedAttention's no-waste allocation, prefix caching — topics 3, 5 and 7. 6·10⁹ / 147 456 ≈ 40 700 tokens in total, ≈ 636 per request at 64 concurrent requests — prompt plus answer. That is why the leaderboard rule is stated in tokens: 64 concurrent requests × (512 prompt + 256 answer) ≈ 49k tokens of KV cache next to the weights, in 16 GB. This particular 4B-in-BF16, 8-KV-head example does not fit. That is model-specific, not a proof that quantization is mandatory: a grouped-query model such as Qwen2.5-3B with 2 KV heads needs only about 36 KiB per token in BF16, so roughly 49k tokens consume about 1.7 GiB of KV cache. Topic 3 treats quantization as one trade-off among model architecture, context, batching and runtime overhead. The ~2 GB runtime figure is a rough allowance (CUDA context, activations, CUDA graphs), not a constant.

Slide L00

The big wok

The fix, in one picture Continuous batching: one wok, many orders. A new order joins at the next toss; a finished plate leaves at the next toss. Nobody waits for the whole table. Preview of topics 4–7. Static batching waits until a batch is full and until its longest answer is done. Continuous (iteration-level) batching re-forms the batch at every decode step: requests enter and leave the running batch individually (Orca, OSDI 2022; vLLM). PagedAttention (vLLM, SOSP 2023) is the counter split into small fixed trays, so no guest reserves space they never use. We do not explain them today — we just watch the effect.

Slide L00

The four numbers we will measure all term

The four numbers we will measure all term Same numbers in the demo, the labs and the leaderboard Metric In the kitchen Definition TTFT time to the first bite time to first token: from sending the request to receiving the first streamed token TPOT pace between courses decode duration divided by post-first-token gaps; related to, but not identical with, an individual inter-token latency Throughput plates per hour output tokens per second, summed over all concurrent requests p95 the slow tail the value 95% of successful requests beat; always report failures beside it i The trade-off you will live in Bigger batches raise throughput and usually hurt TTFT and TPOT. Every configuration choice in this course is a point on that curve. Define these now so the demo reads naturally. Plus two non-negotiables we always report: failed requests (timeouts, OOM) and quality — a fast server that answers wrong is not a server.

Moving it after capture changes nothing. Fri 00:00 02 Clean checkout Exactly that commit, on the judge: 1 × RTX 5070 Ti, nothing left from other runs. clean 03 Start serve.sh (or your Dockerfile) must list submission on /v1/models within one shared 45 min startup budget. ≤ 45 min 04 Quality gate lm-eval against your endpoint: GSM8K, IFEval, MMLU-Pro subsets. ≥ 90% ref 05 Speed GuideLLM at 32 and 64 concurrent clients, 512-token prompts → 256-token answers. The submission contract

The submission contract If I cannot run it from a clean machine, it does not count your-repo/ submission.yaml # model + revision prepare.sh # install + download serve.sh # offline start pyproject.toml # dependencies uv.lock # pinned, reproducible JOURNAL.md # one entry per round Dockerfile # optional: used if present · Model: any open-weight model, with a declared immutable revision, that serves 64 × (512 + 256) tokens at once in 16 GB. · Stack: anything — vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, TensorRT-LLM, your own kernels. serve.sh · example bash #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail exec /runtime/.venv/bin/vllm serve \ Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct \ --revision &lt;immutable-sha&gt; \ --served-model-name submission \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \ --dtype half --max-model-len 4096 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 Fixed: port 8000 , model name submission , streaming /v1/chat/completions with max_tokens , ignore_eos and 4096-token requests. Make a private copy of the public example ; see Start here . The contract is strict on purpose: I must be able to literally clone your repository and run it. prepare.sh gets network access before any secret seed or prompts exist; it installs the locked environment and fetches the declared immutable model revision into the persistent verified model cache; each run receives an isolated serving environment. The measured serve.sh then starts on an internal Docker network with no egress. A Dockerfile is the alternative, but it must bake in everything needed offline. The model and stack may change between rounds. The reference is Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on plain vLLM, FP16: a starting point, not a recommendation. Hidden probes check each response separately, so a high average cannot hide early stopping.

Slide L00

Your dev box is not the judge

Your dev box is not the judge Colab T4 vs RTX 5070 Ti Colab T4 (you) RTX 5070 Ti (judge) Architecture Turing · sm_75 Blackwell · sm_120 VRAM 16 GB GDDR6 16 GB GDDR7 Memory bandwidth 320 GB/s 896 GB/s BF16 · FlashAttention-2 no yes FP8 / FP4 tensor cores no yes ! What this means for you Find a suitable CUDA GPU for development; Colab availability is not guaranteed. FP8 / NVFP4 need compatible hardware. Tuesday startup diagnostics arrive in your private readiness Issue; only judge measurements determine your score. An optimization that wins on the T4 may not transfer, and vice versa: the judge has ~2.8× the memory bandwidth, and supports data types the T4 does not have at all. That is realistic — production hardware is rarely your laptop. Write down in your journal which results came from Colab and which from the judge.

Slide L00

How a round is scored

How a round is scored Gates first, then one number: S Step Rule Snapshot Thursday 23:59 MSK deadline; Friday 00:00 tag snapshot. No round-NN tag → 0. Contract Server lists submission within one shared 45 min startup budget; a streamed smoke answer works. Quality gate GSM8K, IFEval, MMLU-Pro subsets (lm-eval): each ≥ 90% of the reference. Latency & honesty gates p95 TTFT among successful requests at 64 clients ≤ the round's SLO; errors ≤ 1%; every hidden length probe ≥ 95% of 256 tokens. Same model Mean hidden at-rest/load pair similarity ≥ published floor; per-request length and output-diversity checks also pass. Speed \(S = \sqrt{\text{tok/s}_{32} \cdot \text{tok/s}_{64}}\) Mark 0–5 \(5 \times \min(1,\ S / S_{\text{bar}})\); any failed gate → 0. Round = 4% : points = mark × 0.8. Top to bottom, every round. The snapshot makes the deadline real. A server that does not start, or that got fast by getting dumb, scores zero — quality, latency, errors and layered hidden probes are independent gates. Length is checked per hidden response, not by the GuideLLM mean; same-model similarity uses the arithmetic mean of hidden at-rest/load pairs against the published floor (0.8 in Round 01), so one divergent valid continuation need not fail the gate. Diverse prompts must not collapse to one canned output. These are practical anti-gaming checks, not cryptographic proof, so raw artifacts and provenance are retained for audit. Among valid submissions only S matters: the geometric mean of throughput at 32 and 64 clients. The mark is proportional: half the bar = 2.5 of 5. Each round is worth 4% of the course grade (mark × 0.8); ten rounds = 40%.

The defense: tell the story of your kitchen

The defense: tell the story of your kitchen Mandatory · 10% JOURNAL.md · example entry ## Round 04 — prefix caching, more seqs Hypothesis: prompts share a long system prompt → reuse its KV instead of recomputing. Change: --enable-prefix-caching, --max-num-seqs 64 → 96 Judge: c=64 tok/s +30 %, p95 TTFT −0.7 s Kept: yes. Next: FP8 KV cache. · Every change: hypothesis → measurement → decision. · Failed experiments count — they are half the story. · Explain why it worked, not only that it did. The defense is the narrative of your engineering solution: from round 1 to round 10, what you changed, what you expected, what the judge measured, what you kept and what you threw away — and how that path got you to your place on the board. The journal is its raw material; write an entry every round, while you still remember why. The numbers in the example entry are invented for illustration.

No late submissions — a missed round deadline is a 0 for that round. Gaming the benchmark (caching eval answers, special-casing the prompt set, degrading output to win speed) disqualifies the round. The scale is standard. The leaderboard adds one rule of its own: you optimize the server, not the benchmark. The speed prompts are hidden and may rotate; anything that only works because you know the test is disqualified.

Title

LLM SERVING MASTERY Lecture 1 · Foundations Modern LLM inference systems Why one correct generation becomes a queueing, lifecycle, and reliability problem in production. Lecturer Albert Nasybullin Depth System boundary → measurement contract Today we turn “the model answered” into “the service kept a measurable promise under load.”

Slide L01

The 09:00 incident

09:00 · one request was perfect At 08:59 the demo passed. At 09:00 sixty-four clients arrived—and the system began completing work nobody still wanted. Ask what changed. The weights did not. The workload, concurrency, deadlines, and failure feedback did.

Slide L01

One request → one production system

One request → one production system Six decisions 01 Draw the boundary request path and ownership 02 Account for time TTFT, decode, E2E, goodput 03 Specify load arrivals, lengths, saturation 04 Control failure loops queues, deadlines, retries 05 Choose an architecture state, routing, lifecycle 06 Measure, then decide experiment contract and evidence Give the seven turns as a causal investigation: first locate ownership, then define clocks, then offer load, handle failure, choose an architecture, and finally measure it. Ask which turn students expect will explain the 09:00 incident.

Slide L01

By the end, you can diagnose—not guess

By the end, you can diagnose—not guess Observable outcomes 01 Trace a request from arrival to final byte and name every waiting boundary. 02 Compute TTFT, decode time, goodput, concurrency, and retry amplification from raw events. 03 Separate demand, capacity, useful completions, attempts, and failures. 04 Write a reproducible workload/SLO/measurement contract before tuning an engine. Have students name one artifact for each outcome: a boundary diagram, a latency record, a load curve, and a failure policy. These are observable skills, not definitions to memorize.

Slide L01

The 64-client outcome

The 64-client outcome Measured T4 experiment Measured T4 experiment. Count every attempt before explaining latency. These are three burst waves, not a sustained-capacity measurement. Source / method . 192 attempts per path. Serialized pipeline: 38 completions and 154 timeouts. vLLM: 192 completions and zero timeouts. Same GPU and pinned model; three simultaneous waves. Count every attempt before explaining latency. These are three burst waves, not a sustained-capacity measurement. Ask students to describe what is observable and what remains an assumption before proposing a change.

Slide L01

Serving is a promise with a workload attached

Serving is a promise with a workload attached Working definition SYSTEM CONTRACT A serving system accepts demand, schedules stateful generation, streams results, and sheds work so that declared quality, latency, throughput, cost, and availability objectives hold for a declared workload. Remove the workload and the promise is unfalsifiable. Remove failure policy and the promise fails exactly when it matters. Read the promise as a conjunction. A fast answer that is wrong, unavailable, or outside the tenant's deadline does not satisfy the service. Ask what is missing from a bare tokens-per-second figure.

Slide L01

Four questions before any optimization

Four questions before any optimization The diagnostic frame Question Evidence Typical mistake Where? trace and component boundary blame “the model” When? queue/prefill/decode timestamps report one latency Under what load? arrival process + token distributions say “concurrency 32” What happens on failure? deadline, cancel, retry, admission policy let queues grow Use these questions as the diagnostic loop for the incident. If the team cannot identify whose clock or denominator a chart uses, pause before interpreting the number.

Slide L01

Thesis

“ The model call is a stage. The product is the controlled flow around it. Lecture thesis The rest of the lecture earns this sentence with components, equations, and failure cases.

Slide L01

Boundary

01 Draw the system boundary If you cannot point to the queue, you cannot explain the latency. Ask students to draw where the client request first waits. A boundary that starts only at the GPU erases network, admission, queue, and response-stream effects.

Slide L01

Inference is computation; serving is coordination

Inference is computation; serving is coordination Do not collapse the layers Inference tokenize inputs run model forward passes sample next tokens stop on a termination rule Serving authenticate, admit, queue, schedule stream, cancel, retry, rate-limit load, warm, drain, roll back measure promises by tenant/workload Distinguish the model's forward computation from the surrounding control of requests. Ask which side owns cancellation and retry, and why a local completion demo cannot prove service reliability.

Slide L01

Where did 154 requests time out?

Where did 154 requests time out? T4 case study · step with → Client Edge / gateway Admission Scheduler Model worker Telemetry Demand A measured T4 wave sent 64 simultaneous requests, repeated three times: 192 attempts per server. Follow one wave across the boundaries. Edge Both endpoints streamed chat completions. The client waited at most 60 seconds; a working HTTP route did not prove the service could absorb the wave. Admission The serialized baseline offered no effective overload gate: 154 of 192 requests timed out at 64 clients. An early, explicit rejection would be more honest than a silent wait. Scheduler The baseline serialized generation behind one lock. vLLM completed all 192 requests in the same 64-client, three-repeat workload. Worker Both paths served pinned Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in FP16 on the same T4. The model and GPU alone cannot explain the difference. Evidence At 64 clients, p95 TTFT among successful requests was 53.251 s for the baseline versus 0.523 s for vLLM. Failures are counted separately. Measured teaching demo · method and raw records Use the pinned Topic 00 T4 run, not a hypothetical production claim: 64 simultaneous clients × three repeats per server, 60-second client timeout, 154/192 baseline failures versus 0/192 vLLM failures. Ask where a timestamp or rejection policy would localize the wait. The p95 TTFT comparison includes successful requests only; the failed population is separate. The baseline has a single generation lock, not optimized Transformers batching.

Same model, different operating problem

Same model, different operating problem Online vs offline Online arrivals are externally timed per-request deadlines matter streaming and cancellation matter capacity headroom buys reliability Offline batch backlog is controlled completion horizon dominates reordering is often acceptable high utilization can be rational Ask whether the same queue and latency target should be used for a chat turn and an overnight batch job. Common misconception

Common misconception “We put FastAPI around it” What people think “The endpoint is concurrent, therefore the model service is concurrent.” Reveal truth Async HTTP can accept many sockets while all requests wait behind one serialized model path. Generation and delivery clocks

Client disconnect detected at 120 ms, gateway forwards cancellation at 125 ms, scheduler removes the sequence at 140 ms, worker releases request state at 145 ms. These constructed times imply a 25 ms release lag. Cancellation travels toward the worker; release acknowledgement can travel back. Already launched kernels need not stop instantly. Where did the first 323 ms go?

Where did the first 323 ms go? Interactive sequence · budget 300 ms Client Gateway Queue Worker request + auth +8 ms wait admitted +220 ms prefill +90 ms first chunk +5 ms visible token TTFT TTFT budget edge 8 ms queue 220 ms prefill 90 ms transfer 5 ms total 0 Worked example: 8 + 220 + 90 + 5 = 323 ms. Slide L01

TTFT: account for every wait before first content

TTFT: account for every wait before first content Client clock · illustrative serial decomposition $$T_{\mathrm{TTFT}}=T_e+T_q+T_p+T_f$$ T e + T f ms Edge/auth and first visible content transfer T q ms Admission-to-prefill queue residence T p ms Prompt processing + first-token sampling 8 + 220 + 90 + 5 = 323 ms TTFT ; the 300 ms target is missed before streaming begins. Use non-overlapping trace intervals. Real stages can overlap; client TTFT alone cannot separate queue, compute and buffering. TTFT is experienced before any useful streaming cadence. Prefill consumes the known prompt

One output chain advances sequentially

Different requests may advance in the same iteration. For n output tokens there are n−1 gaps after the first output. The first output comes from prompt processing. Count the gaps after the first token

A final protocol acknowledgement can arrive later: \(\mathrm{E2E}=T_{\mathrm{last}}+T_{\mathrm{terminal}}\). The terminal delay follows the last content. Stream chunks need not be single tokens. Name the metric and its interval

Name the metric and its interval No overloaded “latency” Metric Clock interval User question TTFT request → first visible token When does it start? ITL token i → token i+1 Does it stutter? TPOT post-first-token duration / gaps What is average cadence? E2E request → final byte When is it complete? Use one example request to compute TTFT, inter-token gap, and total time. Common metric trap

Common metric trap State the denominator Ambiguous report “TPOT = 22 ms.” Reveal contract Say whether you divide decode duration by output tokens or by post-first-token gaps; say whether you average per request or pool tokens. Different tools use different conventions. Different teams include or exclude the first interval and may report means or percentiles. A percentile needs a population

A percentile needs a population p99 of what? Valid statement p99 TTFT among all admitted chat requests in region A during 10:00–10:15, with failures reported separately. Invalid shortcut “Latency p99 = 1.2 s” with no phase, route, tenant, window, sampling rule, or failure treatment. A p95 is a property of a specified request population and window. Ask how filtering out failures or mixing short and long prompts changes the story.

Slide L01

Goodput counts answers that fulfil the promise

Goodput counts answers that fulfil the promise One observation window · illustrative counts $$G=\frac{N_{\mathrm{useful}}}{\Delta t}$$ G useful req/s Rate of correct, successful, on-time answers N useful requests Unique originals that satisfy all declared SLOs Δt s Wall-clock observation window, including waits 120 complete; 110 correct; 90 also on time in 60 s → G = 90 / 60 = 1.50 req/s . Raw throughput is 120 / 60 = 2.00 req/s. Fix window-edge treatment and count retries separately; this is request-goodput, not token-goodput. Count only successful output that satisfies the declared contract. A burst of invalid or late tokens can raise raw throughput while lowering useful work.

Useful answers in one minute

Useful answers in one minute Illustrative nested populations Illustrative nested populations. Use the same window and original-request population. Retries are attempts, not extra users. 120 completions, of which 110 are correct, of which 90 also meet all SLOs. In 60 seconds: 2.00, 1.83 and 1.50 requests per second respectively. Use the same window and original-request population. Retries are attempts, not extra users. Ask students to describe what is observable and what remains an assumption before proposing a change.

Requests/s and tokens/s answer different questions

Requests/s and tokens/s answer different questions Keep both Request throughput Sensitive to output-length mix. Useful for product capacity when request classes are fixed. Token throughput Exposes generation work, but can rise while user-visible goodput falls. Separate prompt tokens processed from generated tokens delivered. One total tokens-per-second number can reward a different workload instead of a better service.

One symptom, three possible causes Constructed 2-second traces Constructed 2-second traces. The component durations are invented for diagnosis. Measure owner spans before choosing the intervention. The component durations are invented for diagnosis. Measure owner spans before choosing the intervention. Trace durations; do not subtract unrelated clocks

Trace durations; do not subtract unrelated clocks Measurement hygiene Safe monotonic clock within one process span duration recorded by owner synchronized clocks with known error Unsafe client wall clock minus server wall clock mix milliseconds and seconds derive queue time from rounded logs Monotonic timing is for durations; wall time is for correlating events. Explain why subtracting unsynchronized host wall clocks can invent negative queue time.

Slide L01

A real request has more than one clock

A real request has more than one clock Topic 01 · RTX 5070 Ti instructor run Observation Measured value Valid inference Model load 4.51 s exclude from warm request latency 43 input → 63 output tokens 1.395 s non-streaming one local request, no server queue First nonempty text chunk 0.036 s not token-level TTFT Complete streamed response 1.293 s not comparable as a p95 Pinned Qwen2.5-0.5B FP16 · raw teaching evidence · one request, not a capacity test. Do not subtract different request runs to estimate a phase, infer p95 from one request, or call this a server concurrency measurement.

Load

03 Specify the load A benchmark without an arrival process is a demo. The incident began when arrivals changed, not when model weights changed. Translate the 09:00 spike into an offered-work hypothesis to test.

Slide L01

Who controls the next arrival?

Who controls the next arrival? Illustrative traffic clocks Illustrative traffic clocks. Closed loop is a valid user model. It cannot stand in for an independent arrival schedule when overload is the question. An externally scheduled source sends at 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 seconds regardless of responses. A single closed-loop user sends at 0 and again at 3 seconds only after the first response completes. Closed loop is a valid user model. It cannot stand in for an independent arrival schedule when overload is the question. Ask students to describe what is observable and what remains an assumption before proposing a change.

Slide L01

A closed-loop client slows its own offered load

A closed-loop client slows its own offered load Fixed population · one outstanding request per user $$X=\frac{N}{R+Z}$$ X · N req/s · users Completion rate; fixed client population R s Mean full response time, including waiting Z s Mean think time before the next request N = 32, R = 0.5 s, Z = 0.5 s → 32 req/s . If R rises to 1.5 s, X falls to 16 req/s . Steady cycle averages; one request per cycle, no parallel requests per user. A valid user model, but not an independent open-loop arrival schedule. Calculate the rate from clients and response time, then increase response time. The observed request rate falls even as the system deteriorates.

Slide L01

“Concurrency 32” is not a workload

“Concurrency 32” is not a workload Missing dimensions The benchmark claim “We tested at concurrency 32.” Reveal what is missing Arrival model, prompt/output distributions, sampling parameters, streaming, deadline, cancellation, retry policy, warm/cold state, and duration all change the result. Concurrency is live work, not just running GPU kernels. Include queued and streaming requests, then ask what a single concurrency number conceals about token lengths.

Slide L01

Write the workload as a vector

Write the workload as a vector Minimum specification Dimension Example Why it matters arrivals Poisson, 8 req/s burst and queue formation input p50 512, p95 4096 tokens prefill work/state output empirical distribution, cap 256 decode residence policy deadline 5 s, no retry useful demand Specify prompt length, output cap, arrival pattern, and client behavior together. A benchmark whose lengths changed between candidates is not a controlled comparison.

Slide L01

Little’s Law: rate × residence = in-flight requests

Little’s Law: rate × residence = in-flight requests One boundary · the same request population · long-run means $$L=\lambda W$$ L requests Mean queued + running + streaming requests inside the boundary λ requests / s Effective flow through that boundary; not rejected offered traffic W s Mean entry-to-exit time of a request inside the same boundary 8 req/s × 0.5 s = 4 requests in flight on average. At the same rate, 2 s residence implies 16 requests . Stable averages and flow conservation; include all exits consistently. Not λ × p95; not a GPU capacity prediction. Little, 1961 . State the stability assumption before using L = λW. Use the relation to sanity-check averages, not to predict a saturated GPU queue from one point.

Slide L01

Rate, residence and average population

Rate, residence and average population Stable illustrative averages Stable illustrative averages. L = λW uses seconds for W and the same stable flow boundary. It does not determine a peak queue limit. At eight requests per second and half a second average residence, average in-flight count is four. At the same rate and two seconds residence, it is sixteen. More resident work does not imply more throughput. L = λW uses seconds for W and the same stable flow boundary. It does not determine a peak queue limit. Ask students to describe what is observable and what remains an assumption before proposing a change.

Slide L01

Little's Law is an identity—not a capacity model

Little's Law is an identity—not a capacity model What it omits It can tell you whether means are mutually consistent how residence inflates in-flight population which population definition you used It cannot tell you the service-time distribution the saturation knee GPU batching efficiency tail latency or transient behavior When the queue grows during measurement, steady-state assumptions fail. Ask students to plot queue length over the window before using an average latency estimate.

Why waiting explodes near saturation

Why waiting explodes near saturation M/M/1 teaching model · not a continuously batched GPU $$W=\frac{1}{\mu-\lambda},\qquad \rho=\frac{\lambda}{\mu} λ · μ requests / s Arrival rate; service capacity of one server W s Mean time in queue + service for one request ρ dimensionless Utilization; λ must be smaller than μ μ = 10 req/s: λ = 8 → W = 0.5 s ; λ = 9.5 → W = 2 s . Service mean stays 0.1 s. Poisson arrivals; independent exponential service; one server; infinite buffer; steady state. Batching, KV limits and GPU kernels are omitted. This is explicitly not a model of a continuously batched GPU. It builds intuition for nonlinear waiting near saturation.

Slide L01

Waiting near saturation

Waiting near saturation M/M/1 analytical model M/M/1 analytical model. Poisson arrivals, exponential service, one server, unlimited queue, stable rate below 10/s. This curve is not a GPU measurement. With service rate ten requests per second, mean response W = 1/(10−arrival rate). At rates 5, 8, 9 and 9.5, mean response is 0.2, 0.5, 1 and 2 seconds. Mean service stays 0.1 seconds. Poisson arrivals, exponential service, one server, unlimited queue, stable rate below 10/s. This curve is not a GPU measurement. Service time and response time are different clocks

Service time and response time are different clocks Queueing decomposition Service time Time the system actively needs to progress the request, under a precisely defined scheduling model. Response time Queue residence + service + transfers + buffering as observed at the chosen boundary. Separate time spent receiving service from time spent waiting. Faster kernels may not improve the user if queue residence dominates the 09:00 trace.

High GPU utilization is not the objective

High GPU utilization is not the objective Resource metric ≠ product outcome Dashboard comfort “The GPU is at 99%, so the system is efficient.” Reveal truth The GPU can be busy generating late, cancelled, retried, or low-priority tokens. Pair utilization with goodput, queue age, cancellation lag, and SLO attainment. A high utilization sample says the GPU was busy, not whether tokens met deadlines. A low average may hide burst saturation; pair it with queue and latency distributions.

Scheduled requests disappear from a blocking test

A histogram correction cannot reconstruct real queueing, rejection or cancellation outcomes. Source / method . A target schedule has requests at 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 seconds. A blocking client sends only at 0 and 4 while the service stalls. Requests intended at 1, 2, 3 are absent from its histogram, not fast responses. Retain scheduled-send, actual-send and completion times. A histogram correction cannot reconstruct real queueing, rejection or cancellation outcomes. Aggregate percentiles hide workload shifts

Aggregate percentiles hide workload shifts Stratify before comparing Slice Primary stress Compare short in / short out fixed overhead + TTFT admission and batching delay long in / short out prefill input-token bins short in / long out decode residence ITL and cancellation long in / long out state + fairness reject/OOM rates Show why mixing 128-token and 4096-token prompts produces a misleading aggregate. Slide L01

Count attempts, not just original user requests Retry amplification · illustrative stable rates $$\lambda_a=\lambda_o\,\mathbb{E}[A]$$ λₐ · λₒ attempts/s · originals/s Server attempt rate; original user demand A attempts / original Initial attempt plus retries and hedged copies E[A] mean multiplier Average over the same original population 100 originals/s; 20% get one retry → E[A] = 1.2 → 120 attempts/s . Retry storm

Ask when retrying a generation wastes scarce capacity.

New capacity arrives after several separate delays

Slide L02

“Slow GPU” names no mechanism

“Slow GPU” names no mechanism Five competing hypotheses Limiter Constrained quantity Discriminating evidence compute operations/s kernel near compute roof bandwidth bytes/s kernel near memory roof capacity resident bytes allocation failure / eviction launch / shape useful parallel work gaps, tiny kernels, low occupancy queueing admitted demand device fast; request waits outside A bottleneck is the active constraint for a defined workload and phase. Several constraints can appear sequentially.

Slide L02

A percentage is not a diagnosis

A percentage is not a diagnosis What does “GPU 99%” mean? Common inference “Utilization is high, therefore compute is saturated.” Reveal the missing evidence A busy interval may contain memory stalls, tiny kernels, late work, or alternating phases. Diagnose with operations, bytes, shapes, timelines, and counters. NVML-style utilization commonly answers whether kernels were active during sampling windows, not whether tensor cores reached a peak.

Do not jump to a low-level kernel counter before proving which phase and interval matter.

Two residual additions in one decoder block

Two residual additions in one decoder block Qwen2 block · step with → X RMSNorm 1 Attention + first add RMSNorm 2 SwiGLU MLP + second add Input X \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times S\times896}\) Each of S token positions carries 896 values. Preserve X for the first identity bypass. Pinned Qwen2 implementation First norm \(h_1=\operatorname{RMSNorm}(X)\) This starts a branch. The saved X remains unchanged. Pinned Qwen2 implementation Attention branch \(A_{\mathrm{out}}=\operatorname{o\_proj}(A)\) A is the per-head attention output. The branch mixes allowed positions, then projects their features. Pinned Qwen2 implementation First addition \(X_1=X+A_{\mathrm{out}}\) Both inputs have shape [1,S,896]. The upper skip edge carries X unchanged. Pinned Qwen2 implementation Second norm \(h_2=\operatorname{RMSNorm}(X_1)\) The second branch and its bypass both start after the first addition. Pinned Qwen2 implementation MLP branch \(g=\operatorname{gate}(h_2),\quad u=\operatorname{up}(h_2)\) \(M=\operatorname{down}(\operatorname{SiLU}(g)\odot u)\). Elementwise product; each position uses widths 896, 4864, 896. Pinned Qwen2 implementation Second addition \(X_2=X_1+M\) The lower skip edge carries \(X_1\). \(X_2\) enters the next separately parameterized block. Pinned Qwen2 implementation Trace both identity bypasses explicitly. The first addition combines original X and attention output. The second combines X1 and MLP output. RMSNorm acts on the branch before each sublayer; the saved residual is unnormalized. This is a mathematical dependency graph, not a kernel launch schedule. Kernel fusion can combine operations without removing the additions. Every residual has shape [1,S,896].

Slide L03

Know which dimension you quantize

Know which dimension you quantize One down projection · no bias $$Y=XW^\top,\qquad Y_{t,o}=\sum_{i=0}^{4863}X_{t,i}W_{o,i}$$ X [T, 4864] MLP inputs; T token positions after flattening batch W [896, 4864] PyTorch weight: output rows, input columns Y [T, 896] Layer output; not the vocabulary distribution 896 × 4864 = 4,358,144 weights. One row computes one output feature. A group is consecutive input columns within a row; group 64 gives 76 groups per row. Use one output coordinate to explain the sum. T is the total number of recorded positions, not the vocabulary size. Activation values and weights are dimensionless learned quantities. The model takes [1,S,4864] into this layer; we flatten positions only for analysis. A channel here means a feature index, not a token.

AWQ: equivalent channel rescaling

AWQ: equivalent channel rescaling Worked CPU arithmetic · not model measurements $$W'=WD,\quad X'=XD^{-1},\quad X'(W')^\top=XW^\top$$ D [in,in] diagonal One multiplier per input feature X, W [samples,in], [out,in] Divide inputs; multiply columns Multiply weight .49 by 2; divide its input feature by 2. Exact before rounding; not afterwards. AWQ §3.2 . AWQ uses activation information and searches channel scales. This is its equivalent-transformation mechanism, not mixed-precision preservation of a few weights. D is not the scalar quantizer step.
